title: The cycle (Judges 2:11–19)
hook: the people stray, suffer, cry out, and a judge rescues them, again and again

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shechem, and Joshua's people choosing twice. Your line was the stone has heard everything. Today, a new book, and what happens to that choice.

A washing machine has a dial. Wash, rinse, spin, and round again to the start. The book of Judges has one too, and it shows it to you before the first story. Joshua is gone. His generation is gone. And the text says plainly that another generation arose after them, "which knew not the LORD." Nobody rebels in a single dramatic moment. People forget. And from that forgetting, the book sets its dial turning, and it keeps turning for chapter after chapter.
screen: `WASH, RINSE, SPIN, AND ROUND AGAIN.` → `A GENERATION WHICH KNEW NOT THE LORD.` → `THE DIAL STARTS TURNING.`

segments.voice: Chapter two lays out the whole pattern in a few verses, like a summary on the back of a book. First, the people stray: they serve the gods of the land and forsake the Lord who brought them out of Egypt. Second, they suffer: they're handed over to raiders and enemies, and greatly distressed. Third, they cry out; the passage calls it their groaning. Fourth, the Lord raises up a shofet, and the shofet saves them. Then the turn: when the shofet dies, they go back and do worse than their fathers. And the dial comes round again. Shofet is usually translated judge, and the book is called Shoftim, Judges. But in this book a shofet is mostly not someone in a courtroom. The text says the Lord raised up judges who delivered them out of the hand of those who plundered them. A shofet is a rescuer, raised up in a crisis, who leads while they live. Two details are worth slowing down for. Why does God send a rescuer? The text doesn't say the people repented. It says the Lord was moved by their groaning, because of those who oppressed and crushed them. The help comes in answer to pain, before anyone has changed. And the cycle isn't a perfect circle. When each judge dies, the people turn back and act more corruptly than their fathers. Each time round, a little lower. It's a pattern you can watch, and name, and once you see it, recognize in other places.
screen: `STRAY, SUFFER, CRY OUT.` · `A SHOFET IS RAISED UP AND SAVES.` · `MOVED BY THEIR GROANING.` · then, large: `EACH TIME ROUND, A LITTLE LOWER.`

segments.voice: Let one pattern of your own come to mind, small is fine: the late night that leads to the bad morning, the argument that always starts the same way, the promise to yourself that fades by the weekend. Walk it through its stages the way chapter two does: where it starts, where the forgetting is, where it hurts, what you do when it does. Don't fix it now; just see the dial.
Shofet. Judge, in the book of Judges: a rescuer the Lord raises up when the people cry out, who leads them while they live. Today's word.
Your line: the cycle repeats. And each time, a rescuer is raised up. Day seven hundred ten.

howItsDone: Jews read Judges, Shoftim, among the Former Prophets, right after Joshua; its chapter two sets out the pattern of straying, oppression, crying out and rescue that the later stories follow.

chat.says: Judges sounds like courtrooms. What did the judges in that book actually do?
options: Mostly they were rescuers, raised up in a crisis to save the people.
They mostly settled land disputes between the tribes at Shiloh.
They wrote the laws down, since Moses had died without a record.
chat.meaning: The text says the Lord raised up judges who delivered them from those who plundered them: a shofet is mostly a rescuer.

shofet.meaning: judge; in this book, mostly a rescuer raised up in a crisis

Shoftim.meaning: Judges, the Hebrew name of the book

Joshua.meaning: Moses' successor, who led the people into the land

notes: Auditor: 2:11–19 never uses 'cry out' (2:18 has 'groanings'), so the teach now says so; 'each time round, the text says, it goes a little lower' tied to what 2:19 actually says.
Judges 2:10 is quoted from the KJV; JPS 1917 may read 'that knew not the LORD'. Confirm and switch the citation if preferred.
The four stages are this script's teaching summary of 2:11–19, not the text's own numbering.
'Moved by their groaning' paraphrases 2:18 ('it repented the LORD because of their groanings', KJV); translations differ on the verb.
Deborah, who judges cases (4:5), is the exception that comes in two days; not mentioned here.
